mcq.q: For breach of a warranty, the buyer's remedy is:
options: Rejecting the goods and claiming damages
Rejecting the goods only
Rescinding the whole contract
A claim for damages only; he cannot reject the goods
mcq.explain: Under Section 12 a warranty is a subsidiary term, secondary to the main purpose; its breach entitles the buyer to damages, but he must keep the goods. Breach of a condition, which is essential to the main purpose, allows the buyer to treat the contract as repudiated.
mcq.fast: Condition breach = reject + damages. Warranty breach = damages only.

mcq.q: A buyer has accepted goods under a contract that cannot be divided into parts. He later finds that a condition was broken. Under Section 13, he can:
options: Still reject the goods
Rescind the contract and recover the price
Only treat the breach as a breach of warranty and claim damages
Claim nothing at all
mcq.explain: Section 13(2) provides that where a contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, a breach of condition can be treated only as a breach of warranty, unless the contract says otherwise. He therefore loses the right to reject and is left with a claim for damages.
mcq.topic: When a condition is treated as a warranty (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Accepted + non-severable contract -> condition becomes warranty.

mcq.q: Ajay buys a used car from Bimal. Two months later the police take it away because it had been stolen before Bimal got it. Ajay can recover:
options: The full price, as there was a breach of the implied condition as to title
Only the price less two months' use
Nothing, because he used the car
Only nominal damages
mcq.explain: Section 14(a) reads into every sale a condition that the seller is entitled to sell. Bimal had no title, so the condition was broken and the buyer got nothing he bargained for. Following Rowland v. Divall, the buyer can recover the full price despite having used the car, because he never received ownership.
mcq.fast: No title = total failure of consideration = full refund.

mcq.q: Asha asks a chemist for "Brand Z cough syrup" by its trade name and buys it. It does not suit her. Is there an implied condition that it is fit for her purpose?
options: No — when a specified article is bought under its trade name, no condition of fitness for a particular purpose is implied
Yes — the chemist is a dealer, so fitness is always implied
Yes — all medicines carry an implied condition of fitness
No — because medicines are not goods
mcq.explain: Under the proviso to Section 16(1), in a sale of a specified article under its patent or trade name there is no implied condition as to fitness for a particular purpose, since the buyer relies on the brand, not the seller's skill. Caveat emptor applies, though the goods must still be of merchantable quality.
mcq.fast: Bought by trade name = buyer relied on the brand, not the seller -> no fitness condition.

mcq.q: Goods are sold by sample. Which is NOT an implied condition in such a sale?
options: That the bulk corresponds with the sample in quality
That the buyer has a reasonable opportunity to compare the bulk with the sample
That the goods are fit for any purpose the buyer has in mind, even if not disclosed
That the goods have no hidden defect which a fair inspection of the sample would miss
mcq.explain: Section 17 reads three conditions into sales by sample: the bulk has to match the sample, the buyer must have a reasonable chance to compare them, and the goods must be free from hidden defects that a reasonable examination of the sample would not reveal. Fitness for an undisclosed purpose is not implied.
mcq.fast: Sample sale = correspond + compare + no hidden defect. Undisclosed purpose is never protected.

mcq.q: Goods are sold both by sample and by description. The goods delivered match the sample but not the description. The buyer:
options: Can reject them, as the goods must correspond with both — Section 15
Must accept them, as they match the sample
Can only claim damages
Must accept them at a lower price
mcq.explain: Section 15 provides that if the sale is by sample as well as by description, it is not enough that the bulk corresponds with the sample; the goods must also correspond with the description. Since the description, a condition, is not met, the buyer may reject the goods.
mcq.fast: Sample AND description = must match BOTH.

mcq.q: A dealer sells a drum of cleaning chemical that he knows can catch fire if stored near heat. The buyer does not know this, and the dealer says nothing. The drum catches fire and damages the buyer's shop. The dealer is:
options: Not liable, because of caveat emptor
Not liable, as no express warranty was given
Liable only to refund the price of the drum
Liable for breach of the implied warranty to disclose the dangerous nature of the goods
mcq.explain: Where goods are dangerous and the buyer is unaware of it, the seller impliedly warrants that he will warn the buyer of the possible danger. A seller who knows of the danger and stays silent breaches this implied warranty and must compensate the buyer for the resulting damage. Caveat emptor does not protect him here.
mcq.fast: Known danger + buyer unaware + no warning = breach of implied warranty -> damages.

mcq.q: A buyer examined the cloth before buying it. Later he complains about a defect that his examination should have revealed. Under Section 16(2):
options: The seller must take back the cloth
The seller must pay damages
No condition of merchantability applies to defects that his examination ought to have revealed
The contract is void
mcq.explain: Section 16(2) requires goods of saleable (merchantable) quality where they are bought by description from a dealer in that kind of goods. However, a buyer who inspected the goods cannot complain of faults that his inspection should have exposed. Here the buyer carries the risk of what he could have seen.
mcq.fast: Examined + defect visible on examination = buyer's risk.
